title: Why the inside of an uphill bend feels steeper
summary: Both walkways gain the same height, but the inside takes a shorter horizontal route, so its grade is greater. Adjust the road geometry and incline to compare the two paths.
source:
Why the inside of an uphill bend feels steeper

Same total climb; the inside covers less horizontal distance.
R is the radius, not the diameter. Runners follow the centre of each walkway.

Plan view · left turn

Inside walkwayOutside walkway

Rise ÷ horizontal run = grade

Inside
Outside

What matters: wider roads/footpaths and tighter curves increase the difference. The turn angle changes climb and distance, but cancels from grade in this constant-grade circular model. In the straight-road limit (R ≫ d), grades approach equal.

Total climb is equal. At equal speed, the steeper path climbs faster over less distance.

Assumptions: circular centreline of horizontal radius R, constant longitudinal centreline grade g, and both walkway paths gain the same height between radial cross-sections. No changing banking/crossfall; the model is idealised, not a surveyed road. Constant crossfall shifts path heights but does not change their elevation gain; changing banking/crossfall can change the result. Real irregular roads may not satisfy this model.

Model equations & current values

g = p/100; d = w/2 + f/2
Rᵢ = R − d; Rₒ = R + d; θ = a × π/180
H = gRθ; Lᵢ = Rᵢθ; Lₒ = Rₒθ
Inner grade pᵢ = pR/Rᵢ; outer grade pₒ = pR/Rₒ
Relative inner-versus-outer steepness = (Rₒ/Rᵢ − 1) × 100% when p > 0; when p = 0, both level.
Slope angle = atan(gradePercent/100) × 180/π.

Standard grade uses horizontal distance, not surface running distance. Surface distance, if needed, is √(L² + H²).

title: Why the inside of a climbing curve feels steeper
summary: Interactive geometry model comparing inside and outside uphill paths, with live grades, slope angles, rise, distance, and plan- and side-view diagrams.
source:
Why the inside feels steeper

Same rise, shorter run: the inside of an uphill left turn is steeper; the outside is gentler in this geometry model.

Inside path

R must be greater than d. At R = d the inner radius is zero, so this model is not valid.

Local grade · rise/run
Slope angle
Vertical rise
Horizontal path distance

Distance is the plan-view arc, not the sloping surface length. Rise is shared by all three paths over the same turn.

Inside
Outside

● Inside: R − d┄ Centerline: R● Outside: R + d

Plan view · left turn uphill

Horizontal radii shown to relative scale. Travel starts at the bottom and bends left.

Side view · same vertical rise

Changing turn angle changes total rise and distance, not the local grade ratio.

Assumptions, equations & default example

R is the horizontal radius of the centerline. d is the lateral distance from it: inside radius R − d; outside radius R + d. The model assumes R > d.

The road is a smoothly graded surface, with elevation rising at a constant rate along the centerline. All paths have the same elevation at the same turn angle; lateral cross-slope is ignored.

dz = g × R × dθ
Inner grade = g × R / (R − d)
Outer grade = g × R / (R + d)
Rise = g × R × θ
Horizontal path distance = (R ± d) × θ
Slope angle = arctan(grade)

θ and dθ are in radians. In the equations, g and grade are rise/run ratios (6% = 0.06); reported grades are percentages. Use minus for inside, plus for outside.

Default example: R = 40 m, d = 4 m, g = 6%, turn = 90°. Inside: 6.67% (3.81°); outside: 5.45% (3.12°). Centerline: 6% (3.43°). Rise: 3.77 m; inner distance: 56.55 m; outer distance: 69.12 m.

Caution: actual pavement can have cross-slope/banking or uneven grade, and a runner may change line. This model isolates geometry, not medical or safety outcomes.
